dna: Emerged in the 1950s and 60s from a fusion of rock and roll, R&B, and Tin Pan Alley songwriting. Artists like The Beatles, The Supremes, and The Beach Boys shaped its foundations. Pop has continually absorbed new influences — disco, new wave, hip-hop, and electronic music — while keeping accessibility and mass appeal at its core.

Built around the verse-chorus-verse-chorus-bridge-chorus framework, optimised for memorability. Songs typically run 3–4 minutes with the chorus arriving within the first 60 seconds. Pre-choruses build anticipation, and post-chorus hooks extend the earworm factor.

Modern pop relies heavily on synthesizers, drum machines, and programmed beats alongside electric and acoustic guitars. Digital production tools — sampled vocals, sidechain compression, and layered harmonies — are essential. Live strings and brass appear in cinematic arrangements.

The I-V-vi-IV progression dominates, delivering instant familiarity. Catchy melodic hooks, often pentatonic, sit front and centre. Vocal melodies prioritise singability with stepwise motion and memorable intervals. Key changes in the final chorus and call-and-response patterns add emotional lift.

sub.d: Electronic synthesizers replace traditional instruments, delivering sleek, futuristic melodies with pulsing basslines. Depeche Mode, Pet Shop Boys, and The Weeknd carry the torch.
Lo-fi charm meets melodic sensibility. Jangly guitars, understated production, and introspective lyrics from artists like Belle and Sebastian and Vampire Weekend.
Club-ready beats fused with pop hooks. Four-on-the-floor kick drums, euphoric builds, and diva vocals from Madonna to Dua Lipa keep dancefloors moving.
Glitchy synths, vocoder effects, and electronic textures layered over pop song structures. Robyn, Charli XCX, and Grimes push the genre's experimental edges.
High-energy, meticulously produced Korean pop blending hip-hop, R&B, EDM, and pop with precision choreography. BTS, BLACKPINK, and aespa lead the global wave.
Ethereal vocals drenched in reverb, shimmering guitars, and atmospheric washes. Cocteau Twins, Beach House, and Mazzy Star create sonic daydreams.

dna: Born in the 1970s South Bronx, pioneered by DJ Kool Herc isolating breakbeats. Classic boom-bap patterns sit at 70–100 BPM with swung kicks and snares on 2 and 4. Modern trap pushes 130–170 BPM with double-time hi-hats.
Built on the verse-hook-verse framework. Standard verses run 16 bars, hooks span 8 bars, with optional bridges or breakdowns for dynamic contrast. Intros and outros frame the track.

Drum machines define the sound — Akai MPC, Roland SP-404, and the legendary TR-808. Turntables for scratching, samplers for chopping loops, bass synths for sub-heavy low end, and Rhodes keys for melodic warmth.
Thundering 808 bass, rapid hi-hat rolls and triplet patterns, chopped vocal and soul samples, vinyl scratches and crackle, layered trap snares, and pitched-down 808 slides that rattle speakers.

Memphis-inspired, distorted 808s, cowbell patterns, chopped vocal samples, and dark lo-fi textures.

dna: Rooted in the 1950s fusion of blues, country, and rhythm & blues pioneered by Chuck Berry, Little Richard, and Elvis Presley. Built on a driving 4/4 time signature at 100–180 BPM with a strong backbeat on beats 2 and 4.

Classic verse-chorus-verse form with an optional pre-chorus and bridge. Guitar solos typically appear after the second chorus. Power chord progressions and dynamic shifts between quiet verses and loud choruses define the genre.
Electric guitar (often with distortion or overdrive), bass guitar, drum kit (kick, snare, hi-hat, toms, cymbals), vocals, and keyboards or organ in many subgenres.
Power chords (root-fifth dyads) are the backbone. Common progressions include I–IV–V, I–bVII–IV, and i–bVI–bIII–bVII. Pentatonic riffs and blues-based bends add grit and melodic hooks.

sub.d: Guitar-driven anthems with blues roots, melodic solos, and arena-filling energy. Think Led Zeppelin and The Rolling Stones.

Heavy distortion, angst-filled lyrics, and dynamic quiet-loud contrasts. Born in Seattle with Nirvana and Soundgarden.
Extreme volume, distorted guitars, complex riffs, and powerful drumming. Ranging from Black Sabbath to Metallica and beyond.
Lo-fi aesthetics, unconventional song structures, and an independent spirit. Artists like Radiohead and Arctic Monkeys.
Complex compositions, odd time signatures, and conceptual albums. Pioneered by Pink Floyd, Yes, and King Crimson.

dna: Rooted in disco and synth-pop of the late 1970s–80s, EDM exploded through 90s rave culture and 2010s festival boom. Built on a relentless 4-on-the-floor kick pattern, typically 120–150 BPM, with offbeat hi-hats driving the pulse.
Follows the intro → buildup → drop → breakdown → drop arc. Phrases lock to 8- or 16-bar blocks. Sidechaining the bass to the kick creates the signature pumping effect that dominates modern EDM.
Software synthesizers (Serum, Massive, Sylenth1), drum machines (TR-808, TR-909), samplers, and effects processors (reverb, delay, distortion). The DAW itself is the primary instrument.

Layered supersaw chords for euphoria, wobble bass for intensity, risers and impacts for tension, white noise sweeps for transitions, and frequency modulation synthesis for metallic and evolving timbres.

sub.d: The foundation of EDM — four-on-the-floor grooves born in Chicago with soulful vocals, warm basslines, and rhythmic piano stabs.
Hypnotic melodies and long buildups that create euphoric, transcendent experiences on the dance floor.
Heavy sub-bass wobbles and aggressive half-time drops that originated in South London's underground scene.
Breakneck tempos with chopped breakbeats, deep rolling basslines, and roots in UK jungle and rave culture.
Mechanical, hypnotic loops born in Detroit — stripped-back, repetitive, and designed for dark warehouse floors.
Lush, wobbly supersaw chords with pitched vocals and emotional melodic drops blending pop sensibility with electronic production.

dna: Born from Appalachian and Southern folk traditions in the early 1920s, blending Scots-Irish ballads, African American blues, and gospel music. Jimmie Rodgers and the Carter Family laid the commercial foundations. The genre evolved through honky-tonk, the Nashville Sound, and outlaw movements into the diverse landscape heard today.

Story-driven verse-chorus form with a strong narrative arc — country songs are mini short stories. Verses carry the plot, choruses deliver the emotional payoff, and an optional bridge provides a twist or reflection. Lyrics prioritise clarity, specificity, and everyday imagery over abstraction.

Pedal steel guitar and fiddle are the defining timbres. Acoustic guitar (often dreadnought-style) drives rhythm with a classic boom-chuck pattern. Banjo, dobro, mandolin, and harmonica add texture. Modern productions layer electric guitar, bass, and programmed drums.

Built on the I-IV-V chord family with the Nashville Number System as the universal shorthand. Major keys dominate, creating an open, honest feel. Train-beat rhythms, walking basslines, and pentatonic vocal melodies connect the genre to its folk and blues roots.

sub.d: Honky-tonk bars, heartbreak ballads, and the twang of steel guitar. Hank Williams, Patsy Cline, and George Jones defined the golden era of Nashville.
Electric guitars and rock energy meet country storytelling. The Eagles, Gram Parsons, and Chris Stapleton bridge the two worlds.
Rebellious spirit against the polished Nashville Sound. Willie Nelson, Waylon Jennings, and Merle Haggard brought grit, independence, and raw honesty.
A roots-music blend of country, folk, blues, and rock with an emphasis on songwriting craft. Jason Isbell, Brandi Carlile, and Sturgill Simpson lead the movement.
Party anthems mixing hip-hop beats, arena-rock guitars, and country themes of trucks, tailgates, and small-town life. Florida Georgia Line and Luke Bryan popularised the style.
Indie sensibility meets traditional country instrumentation. Uncle Tupelo, Wilco, and Lucinda Williams rejected mainstream polish for authentic, often darker storytelling.

dna: K-Pop traces its roots to Seo Taiji and Boys' 1992 debut, which fused American hip-hop, R&B, and techno with Korean pop sensibility. The Big 3 agencies — SM, YG, and JYP Entertainment — industrialized the idol training system, producing groups like H.O.T., BIGBANG, Girls' Generation, BTS, and BLACKPINK. By the 2010s, K-Pop had become a global cultural force through social media and fandom ecosystems.

K-Pop songs are multi-section compositions that pack genre shifts into a single track. A typical arrangement includes a rap verse, a melodic pre-chorus build, an anthemic chorus, a dance break, and often a dramatic key change or tempo shift near the final chorus. Songs rarely follow a single genre — they weave hip-hop, EDM, R&B, and pop seamlessly within 3–4 minutes.

Production relies on layered synthesizers, trap-influenced 808 drums, EDM-style drops and risers, orchestral stabs, and heavily processed vocal stacks. Live instruments appear as textural accents — electric guitar riffs, brass hits, and string swells. Vocal processing ranges from subtle tuning to aggressive pitch effects and distortion.

Maximalism defines K-Pop production. Tracks feature dense layering, sidechain compression for rhythmic punch, and genre-blending within single songs. Producers like Teddy Park, Yoo Young-jin, and international collaborators stack multiple hooks — vocal, instrumental, and rhythmic — ensuring every section delivers a new earworm. The result is meticulously crafted music engineered for both streaming and live performance.

sub.d: The flagship K-Pop sound: high-energy, choreography-driven music with catchy hooks, group vocal harmonies, and polished production. BTS, BLACKPINK, aespa, and Stray Kids exemplify the modern idol pop format.
Korean hip-hop blending trap, boom-bap, and cloud rap with Korean lyricism. Artists like Jay Park, Zico, and pH-1 bridge underground credibility and mainstream crossover.

Korean rock spanning punk, alternative, and indie. Bands like NELL, DAY6, and FTISLAND blend Korean pop melody with guitar-driven energy and emotional lyricism.
Independent Korean artists creating lo-fi pop, folk, and experimental music outside the idol system. Hyukoh, 92914, and The Black Skirts represent Hongdae's vibrant underground scene.

dna: Rooted in the fusion of African, Indigenous, and European traditions across Latin America and the Caribbean. Defined by clave patterns — the rhythmic key that unlocks every style. Syncopated rhythms, polyrhythmic percussion layers, and infectious grooves span 80–130 BPM across most subgenres.

Verse-chorus frameworks enriched with montuno sections where energy builds through repetition and variation. Call-and-response between lead vocalist (sonero) and chorus (coro), percussion breaks (descargas), and instrumental solos over open vamps.

Congas, bongos, timbales, güiro, maracas, and claves form the percussion core. Tres guitar, piano montuno, and acoustic guitar carry the harmony. Brass sections (trumpet, trombone) deliver melodic hooks, while electric bass and upright bass anchor the low end.

Fluid blending of major and minor keys within single songs. The I–IV–V progression appears everywhere, enriched by chromatic passing chords and modal mixture. Afro-Cuban harmonic patterns, borrowed chords from parallel keys, and rhythmic chord montunos give Latin harmony its unmistakable movement.

sub.d: Born in New York's barrios from Cuban son and jazz, salsa is high-energy dance music driven by clave, piano montuno, and horn arrangements. Popularized by Fania All-Stars, Héctor Lavoe, and Celia Cruz.
Puerto Rican-born fusion of dembow riddims, hip-hop, and dancehall. The signature dembow beat drives modern pop crossover hits from Daddy Yankee, Bad Bunny, and J Balvin.
Brazilian reinvention of samba with cool jazz harmonics, whispered vocals, and nylon guitar. Pioneered by João Gilberto and Antônio Carlos Jobim in late-1950s Rio de Janeiro.
Dominican Republic guitar-driven style with romantic lyrics and a signature bongo pattern. Evolved from bolero roots into a global dance phenomenon through Romeo Santos and Aventura.
Colombian folk dance rhythm blending Indigenous, African, and Spanish elements. Spread across Latin America, producing distinct regional variations from Argentina to Mexico.
Afro-Cuban rhythms meet jazz improvisation and extended harmony. Pioneered by Machito, Dizzy Gillespie, and Tito Puente, bridging the rhythmic intensity of the Caribbean with jazz sophistication.

dna: Rooted in African American musical tradition from the 1940s, R&B evolved through Motown's polished soul, the funk-driven Minneapolis Sound, New Jack Swing's drum-machine grooves, and today's genre-blending modern R&B. Syncopated rhythms and deep pocket define the feel, with tempos typically ranging from 60 to 100 BPM.

Most R&B tracks follow a verse–prechorus–chorus arc, with vocal ad-libs woven throughout. Bridges often introduce a key change or half-time breakdown for emotional lift. An outro vamp — a repeated hook over a fading groove — is a genre staple. Typical song length runs 3 to 5 minutes.

Rhodes and Wurlitzer electric pianos supply the warm harmonic bed. Smooth bass guitar or programmed 808 bass anchors the low end. Programmed drums blend crisp snares with soft hi-hats. Lush string pads, layered vocal harmonies, and the talk box add texture and character.

Melismatic vocal runs and tightly layered harmonies sit at the heart of the R&B sound. Modern productions lean on 808 sub-bass, neo-soul keyboard textures, pitch-shifted vocal chops, and spacious reverb to create an intimate yet cinematic atmosphere.

sub.d: Organic instrumentation meets jazz-inflected harmony and socially conscious lyrics. Defined by Erykah Badu, D'Angelo, and Lauryn Hill.

Hazy, lo-fi-leaning R&B with ethereal vocals, minimalist beats, and heavy reverb. The Weeknd's early mixtapes and How to Dress Well helped define the sound.

dna: "Lo-fi" means low fidelity — embracing imperfection as an aesthetic. The modern lofi movement emerged from bedroom producers in the early 2010s who sampled vintage jazz and hip-hop records. Rhythms feature a relaxed swing groove with off-grid timing, typically sitting between 70–90 BPM.

Tracks are built on simple loops of 4–8 bars that repeat with subtle variations rather than following traditional verse/chorus forms. Textures evolve slowly through layering and filtering, with elements drifting in and out. Most tracks run 2–4 minutes, designed for seamless playlist flow.

Sampled jazz piano and Rhodes electric piano form the harmonic backbone. Drums are muffled and lo-fi processed boom-bap patterns. Tape-saturated bass provides warmth. Vinyl crackle, ambient field recordings (rain, café chatter, birdsong), and pitched-down vocal snippets add atmosphere.

Bitcrushed and pitch-shifted samples give that dusty, aged quality. Sidechain compression creates a gentle pumping feel. Tape wobble and wow/flutter add organic movement. Low-pass filtering softens harsh frequencies. Room reverb, detuned chords, and subtle chorus effects round out the dreamy, hazy character.

sub.d: The core lofi sound — mellow sampled beats with jazzy chords, vinyl texture, and laid-back boom-bap drums. Popularized by YouTube livestream culture.
A brighter, more polished cousin of lofi hip-hop with live-sounding instrumentation, upbeat grooves, and jazzier arrangements.
Heavily jazz-influenced beats rooted in Nujabes and J Dilla's legacy. Prominent use of jazz samples, complex chord progressions, and soulful melodies.
Applies lofi's dusty, lo-fidelity aesthetic to house music. Warped disco samples, grainy textures, and hypnotic repetition over four-on-the-floor kicks.
Ultra-minimal lofi designed to fade into the background. Sparse arrangements, very soft dynamics, and long ambient pads optimized for focus and concentration.
Lo-fi recording techniques applied to indie pop songwriting. Hazy vocals, simple chord progressions, and DIY production charm from artists like Clairo and Boy Pablo.

dna: Rooted in early 1900s New Orleans, shaped by African American communities blending African rhythms, blues, and ragtime. Defined by swing feel, syncopation, and polyrhythmic interplay. Typical tempos range from 60 BPM ballads to 300+ BPM bebop burners.

Standard forms include 32-bar AABA (Tin Pan Alley standards), 12-bar blues, and open modal vamps. Tunes state the head (melody), open up for improvised solos over the chord changes, then return to the head to close.
Saxophone (alto, tenor, soprano), trumpet, trombone, piano, double bass, drum kit with ride cymbal, vibraphone, and guitar. The rhythm section (piano, bass, drums) anchors every ensemble.

The ii–V–I progression is the backbone of jazz harmony. Extended voicings with 7ths, 9ths, 11ths, and 13ths add color. Tritone substitutions, diminished passing chords, and chromatic voice leading create the genre's rich harmonic language.

sub.d: Fast, virtuosic improvisation with complex chord changes and angular melodies pioneered by Charlie Parker and Dizzy Gillespie.
Polished, radio-friendly sound with soft electric keyboards, light funk grooves, and melodic saxophone leads.
Built on scales rather than chord changes, creating spacious and meditative improvisation. Defined by Miles Davis's Kind of Blue.
Relaxed tempos, lighter tone, and arranged textures from the West Coast scene. Think Chet Baker and Dave Brubeck.
Jazz meets rock and funk — electric instruments, complex meters, and high-energy improvisation from Weather Report to Snarky Puppy.
Abandons fixed harmony and meter for collective improvisation and radical expression. Pioneered by Ornette Coleman and John Coltrane.
